blocks.text: 1. Batch Prediction

blocks.alt: A large dataset runs through a batch job into a predictions file

blocks.text: Inference Pipeline, the previous topic, previewed both Batch and Real-Time serving patterns as two different ways of calling the same underlying pipeline object. Batch Prediction runs that pipeline across many rows together, all at once, rather than handling one request at a time.

It is typically triggered on a schedule, nightly, hourly, or whenever new data arrives in bulk, and the resulting predictions are written somewhere for later use, a database table or a file, rather than returned immediately to a waiting caller the way a real-time request would be.
2. When Batch Prediction Fits Naturally

blocks.alt: No immediate response needed points toward batch prediction fitting well

blocks.text: Batch prediction fits naturally when no immediate response is needed, generating tomorrow's recommendation list for instance, where latency simply does not matter since the results get consumed later, not the instant they are computed. It also fits when a large volume of data needs scoring together, scoring an entire customer base overnight for example, where processing in bulk is far more efficient than handling one request at a time.

And it fits naturally when the prediction genuinely depends on data that is only available in bulk in the first place, computing a metric from a full day's accumulated transactions for instance, where real-time serving would not even have the needed data available yet at the moment any single request arrived.
3. The Batch Prediction Flow

blocks.alt: A scheduled job loads the model, scores all rows, then saves results

blocks.text: A typical batch prediction flow begins when a scheduled job triggers, every night at 2 AM for instance, a time deliberately chosen to avoid peak usage hours. That job loads the serialized Inference Pipeline covered in the previous topic, exactly the same bundled preprocessing-plus-model object used everywhere else.

It then loads a large batch of new, unscored rows, often millions of rows at once, runs pipeline.predict a single time across that entire batch, and writes all of the resulting predictions to a database table or file, ready for whatever downstream system or report needs to consume them next.

blocks.text: 4. The Efficiency Advantage

blocks.alt: Batch prediction processes many rows at once

blocks.text: Processing rows one at a time incurs repeated overhead on every single request, connection setup, function call overhead, and repeated small computations that do not benefit from any economy of scale. Batch processing amortizes that overhead across many rows processed together in one single operation instead.

Vectorized operations, NumPy array math for instance, are considerably faster on large batches than performing the equivalent computation on single rows one after another, since vectorized code can take advantage of optimized, low-level array operations rather than repeating Python-level overhead for every individual row. This produces a genuine, measurable throughput advantage over real-time serving specifically for large volumes of data.
5. The Staleness Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Batch prediction results can be hours old

blocks.text: The real tradeoff batch prediction accepts is that predictions are only ever as fresh as the last scheduled run. A customer's behavior changing right after last night's batch run completes goes entirely unreflected in any prediction until the next scheduled run actually happens.

This staleness is genuinely fine for many use cases, a weekly churn risk score does not need to update every single second to remain useful. But it is a real, meaningful problem for others, fraud detection for instance needs Real-Time Prediction, the very next topic in this module, rather than batch, since a fraudulent transaction needs to be caught the moment it happens, not the next time a scheduled job happens to run.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Before choosing batch prediction for any given use case, explicitly ask how stale a prediction is allowed to be. If the honest answer is "not stale at all," Real-Time Prediction, covered next, is very likely the correct choice instead.

blocks.text: 6. A Typical Infrastructure Pattern

A typical batch prediction infrastructure setup relies on a workflow scheduler, cron for simple cases or a more full-featured tool like Airflow for complex, multi-step pipelines, to trigger the job at the appropriate time.

The job itself runs on a compute cluster sized specifically for the batch's volume, then shuts down entirely once the run completes. This means no server needs to stay running and waiting idle between batch runs, a meaningful cost advantage over the always-on server infrastructure Real-Time Prediction, covered next, actually requires.
7. Handling Failures Gracefully

blocks.alt: A batch job that fails partway retries from a checkpoint

blocks.text: A batch job processing millions of rows will, in practice, encounter some genuinely bad rows along the way, a malformed value, an unexpected data type, a field that violates an assumption the pipeline relies on. A single malformed row should not be allowed to silently crash the entire job and lose all of the otherwise-valid predictions computed alongside it.

The better practice is to log and skip individual bad rows while still completing the rest of the batch successfully, then report a clear summary at the end, how many rows were processed successfully, how many were skipped, and why each one was skipped, giving whoever reviews the job's output a genuinely actionable picture of what happened.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A batch job that fails 100 percent or succeeds 100 percent with no partial-failure handling in between is a fragile design. Real production data almost always contains at least a few genuinely bad rows.

blocks.text: 8. Connecting to Monitoring

This connects forward to Monitoring, an upcoming topic later in this Model Deployment module. Every batch run should log key operational facts: how many rows were processed, how long the run took, and how many rows failed or were skipped.

A batch job that silently stops running altogether, due to a scheduler misconfiguration or an unnoticed upstream failure, is a real, surprisingly common production failure mode, one that can go unnoticed for days if nothing is actively monitoring whether the expected batch actually ran and produced the expected volume of output.
9. When Batch Prediction Is the Right Choice

blocks.alt: Large volume with no urgency points toward using batch prediction

blocks.text: Batch Prediction is the right choice for scoring an entire customer base for a marketing campaign, where no individual request is actively waiting and the results simply feed a downstream system, an email campaign tool for instance, at a later point in time.

It similarly fits generating daily reports or dashboards from model output, where the underlying data is naturally consumed in bulk rather than one prediction at a time. Whenever an immediate, per-request answer is genuinely required instead, Real-Time Prediction, covered in the very next topic, is the better fit.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below simulates a batch prediction job, loading a pipeline, scoring a large batch of rows at once, and gracefully handling a few malformed rows along the way.

code.content:
import joblib
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

pipeline = joblib.load("inference_pipeline_v1.joblib")

rng = np.random.RandomState(7)
batch = pd.DataFrame({
    "feature_a": rng.normal(size=10000),
    "feature_b": rng.normal(size=10000),
})
batch.loc[rng.choice(10000, 15, replace=False), "feature_a"] = np.nan  # a few bad rows

valid_mask = batch.notna().all(axis=1)
valid_rows = batch[valid_mask]
skipped_count = (~valid_mask).sum()

predictions = pipeline.predict(valid_rows.values)

results = pd.DataFrame({"row_id": valid_rows.index, "prediction": predictions})
print(f"Batch complete: {len(predictions)} rows scored, {skipped_count} rows skipped")
print(f"Sample predictions:\n{results.head()}")
results.to_csv("batch_predictions.csv", index=False)
print("Results written to batch_predictions.csv for downstream use")

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This example intentionally skips rows with missing values rather than crashing on them, then reports exactly how many rows were skipped, mirroring the graceful failure handling covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Batch Prediction runs the Inference Pipeline across many rows together, typically on a schedule, writing results for later use.
It fits use cases with no immediate response needed, large volumes to score, or data only available in bulk.
The flow: scheduled trigger, load the pipeline, load a large batch, predict once across everything, write results.
Amortized overhead and vectorized computation give batch a real throughput advantage for large volumes.
Predictions are only as fresh as the last scheduled run, fine for many cases, unacceptable for latency-sensitive ones.
A workflow scheduler triggers sized compute that shuts down between runs, no server needs to stay always-on.
A single bad row should not crash the whole job; log and skip individual failures, then report a clear summary.
Every batch run should log rows processed, duration, and failures, connecting to the Monitoring topic later in this module.
Next up: Real-Time Prediction, serving a single request immediately when staleness is not acceptable.
